result: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated vsx1 and vsx2 double knockout zebrafish (vsxKO) were successfully generated with deletions in the DNA-binding domain. The vsx1Δ245 mutation results in an in-frame deletion of 53 amino acids, while vsx2Δ73 deletes 24 amino acids and generates a premature stop codon. Western blot confirmed absence of both Vsx1 and Vsx2 proteins in vsxKO embryos at 24hpf, with no maternal Vsx1 detected.
evaluation: Claims C40-C45 provide comprehensive molecular characterization of the mutants with genomic deletions, protein structure predictions, and western blot validation. The mutations target conserved DNA-binding domains and result in loss of detectable protein, establishing these as likely null alleles. The experimental evidence is internally consistent and well-documented.

result: vsxKO zebrafish embryos display normal eye morphology and size without microphthalmia, contrasting with mammalian vsx mutants. Single mutants and heterozygotes reach adulthood and are fertile, while double mutants die around 3 weeks post-fertilization. Neural retina is properly specified and maintained in vsxKO embryos.
evaluation: Claims C46-C48 and C8-C9 are well-supported by histological observations and survival data across multiple developmental stages. The absence of microphthalmia is documented through multiple imaging modalities and quantitative measurements (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, 3). This represents a key species difference from mice and is a major finding of the study.

result: vsxKO retinas show progressive lamination defects during development. At 48hpf, there is a small delay in IPL formation. By 72hpf, both OPL and IPL appear disorganized with discontinuities. At 6dpf, ONL thickness is significantly increased while INL thickness is significantly reduced compared to wildtype.
evaluation: Claims C49-C51 describe a temporal progression of retinal lamination defects supported by histological sections at multiple timepoints (Figure 1b-h). The quantification of layer thickness at 6dpf (Figure 1—figure supplement 3i) provides statistical support for the INL/ONL changes. The progression from subtle to overt defects is well-documented.

result: vsxKO fish exhibit expanded melanocyte pigmentation even under bright light exposure, indicative of impaired visual background adaptation (VBA) reflex and associated with blindness in zebrafish.
evaluation: Claims C52-C53 are supported by visual observations (Figure 1e, i; Figure 1—figure supplement 3a, d) and citation to established knowledge linking VBA defects to blindness. The phenotype is clear and consistent across multiple animals, providing a behavioral readout of visual impairment.

result: ERG recordings reveal severe visual impairment in vsx mutants. vsx2Δ73 shows normal responses similar to WT. vsx1Δ245 shows reduced b-wave amplitude. In vsxKO double mutants, 26/36 larvae show only a-wave with no b-wave, while 10/36 show reduced b-wave. Statistical analysis confirms significantly decreased b-wave in vsx1Δ245 and vsxKO compared to WT at all light intensities, with vsxKO more severely affected than vsx1Δ245.
evaluation: Claims C55-C61 are strongly supported by ERG data (Figure 2a, b) with appropriate sample sizes (n=6-36) and statistical analysis. The b-wave represents bipolar cell function, and its reduction/absence directly supports the bipolar cell defect. The graded severity (WT > vsx2 ≈ WT > vsx1 > vsxKO) is internally consistent and statistically validated.

result: Optokinetic response (OKR) measurements show significant reduction in eye velocity for vsx1 single and vsxKO double mutants compared to vsx2Δ73 and WT controls across all tested conditions (contrast, spatial frequency, temporal frequency).
evaluation: Claim C62 is supported by comprehensive OKR testing (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) with appropriate statistical analysis (ANOVA p<0.001). The consistency across multiple stimulus parameters strengthens the conclusion of visual impairment. Sample sizes are adequate (n=9-18).

result: Proliferation analysis reveals temporal dysregulation in vsxKO retinas. At 24 and 48hpf, PH3+ cell numbers are normal. At 60hpf, vsxKO shows significantly increased PH3+ cells in outer and peripheral regions when WT proliferation has largely ceased. By 72hpf, proliferation returns to normal levels restricted to the CMZ.
evaluation: Claims C63-C65 are supported by PH3 immunostaining at multiple timepoints (Figure 3a-f, m) with quantification and statistical analysis. The temporal pattern of extended proliferation at 60hpf followed by normalization at 72hpf is clearly documented. This suggests a delay rather than a permanent proliferation defect.

result: Apoptosis analysis shows increased cell death in vsxKO retinas at later stages. At 60hpf, C3+ cells are rare in both WT and vsxKO. At 72 and 96hpf, vsxKO shows significantly increased C3+ cells concentrated mainly in the INL, with some apoptotic cells also in the GCL.
evaluation: Claims C66-C69 are supported by caspase-3 immunostaining (Figure 3g-l, n) with quantification showing significant increases at 72 and 96hpf. The spatial localization to INL is consistent with the reduced INL thickness observed histologically. The temporal onset after 60hpf suggests secondary consequences of failed bipolar cell differentiation.

result: Retino-tectal projections appear normal in vsxKO larvae at 6dpf based on DiI/DiO tracing, indicating that retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) are not affected.
evaluation: Claim C70 is supported by DiI/DiO tracing experiments (Video 1) with adequate sample sizes (n=6 WT, n=8 vsxKO). The 3D reconstructions show apparently normal projection patterns. However, the assessment is qualitative ('no obvious differences') rather than quantitative, which limits the strength of the conclusion.

result: Photoreceptor differentiation is delayed in vsxKO retinas. The transient marker prdm1a shows mild downregulation at 72hpf. Terminal differentiation markers Zpr-1 (cones) and Zpr-3 (rods) show delayed expression at 72 and 96hpf, with Zpr-1 significantly increased at 6dpf in vsxKO compared to WT.
evaluation: Claims C71-C73 are supported by in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry data (Figure 4a, e; Figure 4—figure supplement 1) with quantification. The temporal delay in differentiation markers is clearly documented, and the eventual increase in cone marker intensity suggests fate rerouting toward photoreceptors. This is consistent with the expanded ONL thickness.

result: Bipolar cell specification is severely compromised in vsxKO retinas. While prox1 expression appears normal at 48hpf, its nuclear distribution in the INL is affected at 72hpf. The bipolar cell marker prkcbb is very reduced or absent in the INL at 72hpf. These findings confirm that vsx genes are essential for bipolar cell specification in zebrafish.
evaluation: Claims C74-C77 are strongly supported by in situ hybridization data (Figure 4b, f; Figure 4—figure supplement 2). The loss of prkcbb expression is dramatic and consistent with the ERG findings of reduced/absent b-wave. Claim C77 represents a key conclusion that integrates multiple lines of evidence (histology, ERG, molecular markers).

result: Amacrine cell specification appears unaffected in vsxKO retinas. The transient marker ptf1a shows normal expression at 48 and 72hpf, and the differentiated marker pax6 is not affected. This suggests vsx genes do not play a major role in amacrine cell specification in zebrafish.
evaluation: Claims C78-C80 are supported by in situ hybridization data (Figure 4c, g; Figure 4—figure supplement 2c, d, g, h). The normal expression of both early and late amacrine markers across multiple timepoints provides strong evidence. However, the conclusion (C80) is stated cautiously as 'do not play a major role' rather than 'no role,' which is appropriate given the data.

result: Müller glia cells are overrepresented in vsxKO retinas, as evidenced by a clear increase in gfap expression compared to WT. This may compensate for the reduction in bipolar cells.
evaluation: Claims C81-C82 are supported by in situ hybridization data (Figure 4d, h) showing increased gfap expression. The inference that this represents overrepresentation and potential compensation (C82) is reasonable given that Müller glia and bipolar cells share common progenitors. However, quantification of cell numbers would strengthen this conclusion.

result: V2 spinal cord interneurons are properly specified in vsxKO animals. No significant differences in V2a or V2b interneuron density were observed at 24hpf, and obvious swimming defects were not observed in vsxKO larvae.
evaluation: Claims C83-C85 are supported by in situ hybridization data (Figure 4—figure supplement 3) with quantification showing no significant differences. The normal swimming behavior is consistent with proper spinal interneuron specification. This addresses whether the lethality at 3 weeks is due to motor defects (apparently not).

result: Early retinal specification appears largely normal in vsxKO mutants. Optic cup morphology, size, proliferation rate, and RPE markers (tfec, bhlhe40) are normal at 24hpf. The only altered parameter is a slight delay in retinal differentiation onset as shown by atoh7 expression at 26hpf.
evaluation: Claims C86-C87 are supported by PH3 staining and ISH data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). The comprehensive assessment of multiple early parameters strengthens the conclusion that early specification is intact. The slight delay in atoh7 is a subtle phenotype that may presage later defects.

result: ATAC-seq at 18hpf identified 1564 differentially accessible chromatin regions in vsxKO vs WT, with 633 more accessible (log2FC >1.5) and 571 less accessible (log2FC <-1.5). Gene ontology analysis of 2219 genes neighboring these regions revealed enrichment for neuronal differentiation and eye development terms, suggesting vsx mutation causes deregulation of hundreds of cis-regulatory elements associated with retinal genes.
evaluation: Claims C88-C92 are supported by ATAC-seq data (Figure 5a, b) with appropriate bioinformatic analysis. The large number of differentially accessible regions indicates substantial chromatin remodeling. The GO enrichment for eye-related terms validates the biological relevance. However, the functional significance of these changes requires integration with transcriptomic data.

result: RNA-seq at 18hpf revealed relatively modest transcriptional changes in vsxKO vs WT, with only 1018 differentially expressed genes. Among genes with high fold change (log2FC >|1.5|), only 41 were upregulated and 31 downregulated, including just 3 upregulated TFs (vsx1, znf1109, znf1102) and 1 downregulated TF (znf1091). Importantly, only 5% (119/2219) of genes neighboring differentially accessible chromatin regions showed differential expression.
evaluation: Claims C93-C96 are supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 5c, d) with appropriate analysis. The disconnect between chromatin accessibility changes (1564 regions) and transcriptional changes (72 genes with log2FC >|1.5|) is striking and well-documented. This is a key finding suggesting network robustness. The low overlap (5%) between ATAC and RNA-seq hits is particularly informative.

result: qPCR analysis of core retinal specification genes at 19hpf showed significant expression changes only for rx2 and lhx2b (below log2FC >|1.5| threshold) in vsxKO embryos. The mutated genes vsx1 and vsx2 were significantly upregulated and downregulated respectively. These analyses suggest the general architecture of the retinal GRN was not significantly altered by vsx mutation.
evaluation: Claims C97-C99 are supported by qPCR data (Figure 5e) and ISH validation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). The minimal changes in core retinal TFs despite extensive chromatin remodeling supports the network robustness hypothesis. The upregulation of vsx1 transcript in vsxKO is interesting but doesn't rescue the phenotype, suggesting post-transcriptional or functional insufficiency.

result: Comparison of vsxKO mutants with vsx2 morphants revealed very different regulatory responses. PCA analysis showed clear separation between mutant and morphant samples. Core retinal network genes (rx3, rx1, six3b, vax2, lhx2b) were upregulated in morphants but not mutants. vsx2 itself was strongly downregulated in mutants but upregulated in morphants. This suggests morpholino-induced dysregulation of the retinal network underlies the microphthalmia observed in morphants.
evaluation: Claims C100-C103 are supported by RNA-seq comparison (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) with PCA and heatmap visualization. The stark differences between mutant and morphant transcriptomes explain the phenotypic discrepancy and highlight potential off-target or compensatory effects of morpholinos. This is an important validation of the genetic approach and explains previous conflicting results.

result: CRISPR/Cas9 mutations in medaka vsx1 (Δ148bp) and vsx2.1 (Δ319bp) were generated, both causing frameshift mutations affecting the DNA-binding domain. While initial organ specification appeared normal at 4dpf, INL differentiation and eye growth were impaired at later stages, resulting in microphthalmia. This contrasts with normal eye size in zebrafish vsxKO at 19dpf and confirms variable regulatory weight for vsx genes across vertebrate species.
evaluation: Claims C105-C112, C104, C138 are supported by medaka mutant generation and histological analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 3). The comparative analysis between zebrafish and medaka is compelling, showing that even within teleosts there is variation in vsx requirement. However, the medaka analysis is less comprehensive than the zebrafish work, and the third paralog (vsx2.2) was not mutated, which could affect interpretation.

result: Vsx activity is essential for bipolar cell differentiation in teleost fish, indicating a broadly conserved role across vertebrates. This suggests the genetic program controlling bipolar specification was inherited from a common vertebrate ancestor. Expression of Vsx homologs in invertebrate visual systems (Drosophila, Cuttlefish) further suggests this function may be conserved across all metazoans.
evaluation: Claims C113-C114 are well-supported by the zebrafish data showing bipolar cell loss. C115-C116 extend this to invertebrates based on citations, but this is more speculative. The evolutionary inference (C114, C116) is reasonable but goes beyond what the data directly demonstrate. The claim about 'all metazoans' (C116) is particularly speculative given limited sampling.

result: In vsxKO retinas, precursors unable to acquire bipolar fate follow alternative trajectories including apoptosis, extended proliferation, or differentiation as photoreceptors or Müller glia. The photoreceptor fate bias agrees with mouse studies showing Blimp1/Vsx2 antagonism controls rod/bipolar balance. Vsx activity is required both for correct fate specification and for determining the timing of differentiation.
evaluation: Claims C117-C119 integrate multiple lines of evidence (apoptosis, proliferation, marker expression) to infer fate trajectories. The agreement with mouse studies (C118) strengthens the interpretation. The timing defect (C119) is well-documented by the delayed expression of photoreceptor markers. This represents a comprehensive model of the vsxKO phenotype.

result: Bipolar and glial cells are late-born retinal types from common progenitors with restricted potential. In mice, significant Müller glia increases have not been reported in vsx mutants (postnatal or bipolar-specific), though a trend toward increase has been noted.
evaluation: Claims C120-C122 are based on citations to previous literature and provide context for interpreting the zebrafish Müller glia increase. The citations appear appropriate. However, this represents background knowledge rather than new findings from this study.

result: Neuro-retinal identity is maintained in vsxKO double mutants with no trans-differentiation to pigmented cells detected. This contrasts with mouse microphthalmia and specification defects, suggesting vsx genes do not play an early role in establishing/maintaining neural retina identity in zebrafish. Maternal rescue is unlikely as vsx transcripts are not detectable before zygotic genome activation.
evaluation: Claims C123-C126 are supported by histological observations and citation (C126). The absence of RPE trans-differentiation is well-documented. The inference about lack of early role (C125) is reasonable given the data, though alternative explanations (redundancy) are also discussed. The exclusion of maternal rescue (C126) is important for interpretation.

result: Poor resemblance between morpholino and mutant phenotypes has been described in zebrafish, with genetic compensation/transcriptional adaptation identified as a mechanism for genetic robustness. However, comparative transcriptomic analysis of vsxKO vs WT does not support genetic compensation as a relevant mechanism at optic cup stages.
evaluation: Claims C127-C128 cite relevant literature on morpholino/mutant discrepancies and compensation mechanisms. C129 is supported by the RNA-seq data showing minimal upregulation of related genes. The absence of classic compensation signatures (upregulation of paralogs or related genes) is an important negative result that points toward network redundancy instead.

result: The zebrafish eye specification regulatory networks are remarkably robust. The consensus motif 5'-TAATT-3' is central to neural retina cis-regulatory logic and is shared by many homeodomain TFs (vsx1, vsx2, rx1, rx2, rx3, lhx2b, lhx9, hmx1, hmx4) co-expressed during retinal specification. These TFs may co-regulate genes and cooperate within cis-regulatory modules. Gene redundancy appears as the most parsimonious explanation for the absence of early phenotype in vsxKO.
evaluation: Claims C130-C133 are supported by citation to previous work (Buono et al., 2021) and represent the authors' mechanistic interpretation. The redundancy model (C133) is well-supported by the data showing extensive chromatin changes with minimal transcriptional impact and normal early specification despite vsx loss. This is a key conceptual contribution of the paper.

result: Other mutations in TFs targeting the 5'-TAATT-3' motif (rx2 in medaka, lhx2 in zebrafish) do not compromise neural retina identity. Even in mouse vsx1/vsx2 double mutants, central retina retains potential for neuronal differentiation. In mouse Vsx2 mutants, neural retinal defects and microphthalmia can be partially restored by deleting a cell cycle gene.
evaluation: Claims C134-C136 are based on appropriate citations and provide comparative context supporting the redundancy model. The examples from other species strengthen the argument that no single TF in this network is absolutely required. However, these represent prior knowledge rather than new findings.

result: Genetic redundancy is an important mechanism sustaining the integrity of the retinal specification network. Vsx genes' regulatory weight varies substantially among vertebrate species.
evaluation: Claims C12-C13 represent the major conceptual conclusions of the paper. They are well-supported by the integration of multiple lines of evidence: (1) extensive chromatin remodeling with minimal transcriptional impact, (2) normal early specification despite vsx loss in zebrafish, (3) differences between zebrafish and medaka, (4) contrast with mouse phenotypes. These are appropriately stated as inferences from the data.
